I'm Wasim. When my father was in hospital last winter, my friend Devika did something I still can't get over. She took over my sister's wedding preparations for a whole month: forty phone calls to caterers, two trips to Lucknow for the lehenga, a spreadsheet for the guest list that my entire family still uses.

At the wedding I tried to thank her. She laughed. "Arre, it was nothing. Anyone would have done it."

The old me would have argued. "No, really, it was huge!" and she'd have said "no, no," and we'd have gone round and round till the thanks disappeared.

This time I just said it plainly. "Devika, it was forty calls and two trips to Lucknow while you had your own job. That's a lot. Thank you." And then I stopped talking.

She opened her mouth, then closed it. She looked at the mehendi on her hands for a while.

"Okay," she said quietly. "You're welcome."

qa.q: How many phone calls did Devika make to caterers?
qa.a: Forty phone calls.

qa.q: What might Devika have been feeling when she looked at the mehendi on her hands for a while?
qa.a: She may have felt awkward and a little moved, not used to having her effort named so clearly. Being unable to wave it away probably made the thanks land.

qa.q: Why did stopping talking after the thank-you work better than arguing?
qa.a: Arguing would have started the usual back-and-forth that made the thanks disappear. Naming the effort once and then staying quiet let the words stay with Devika.

qa.q: How did Devika's help affect Wasim's family, beyond the wedding day?
qa.a: The whole family still uses her guest-list spreadsheet, and her help carried them through while Wasim's father was in hospital. That is why the thanks mattered so much to Wasim.

Coordinator's note, animal shelter, Sunday evening

Today's adoption day placed nine dogs, our best ever. Lakshmi, one of our volunteers and a friend of mine since college, organised almost all of it: posters, the vet table, the forms, the volunteer rota. She was here at six this morning.

When the director thanked her at the end in front of everyone, Lakshmi said, "Oh, it's nothing. Everyone helped." She said something similar to three adopting families.

Afterwards, while we were rolling up mats, I said to her, "Lakshmi, you made the rota for twenty people, you came at six, and nine dogs went home. That took real effort. Thank you." I didn't add anything, and I didn't let her change the subject for a moment.

She went quiet. Then she said, "It did take a lot." She sounded surprised hearing herself say it.

Next step: I'll put her name on the thank-you board this week, and ask her to lead the next adoption day.

— Sangeeta

qa.q: How many dogs were placed at today's adoption day?
qa.a: Nine dogs.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi saying "It did take a lot" and sounding surprised suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she rarely lets herself admit her own effort, and hearing Sangeeta name it clearly let her see it too. The surprise shows how unusual it was for her to accept the praise.

qa.q: What made Sangeeta's thanks different from the director's?
qa.a: Sangeeta named specific efforts, the rota for twenty, arriving at six and nine dogs going home, and then stopped without letting the subject change. That made it hard for Lakshmi to wave away.

qa.q: How might the three adopting families feel about Lakshmi, even if she said it was nothing?
qa.a: They probably felt grateful and saw her as the one who made the day work. Their thanks was real even when Lakshmi brushed it off.

grounding: A friend who coordinates volunteers notes a young woman deflecting praise as nothing, then names her specific effort and lets the thanks stay.

Omkar opened his mouth. The old words were ready: It's just the masala, anyone can make it.

I'm Vinita. Until last year, if anyone praised my work, I had a reflex: "Oh, it was the team." "It was easy." "I just got lucky." My friend told me it was actually exhausting to watch. "You're a brilliant woman who talks like a nervous intern," she said.

So in January I made two small rules.

One: when someone compliments me, I say "thank you" and nothing else. No explaining it away.

Two: I keep a private note on my phone called "Things that went well." Just facts.

The first test came in February. Tejas, our senior analyst, stopped by my desk and said, "Your flood-risk report was the clearest one we've had." My mouth started to say "the data was easy." I bit it back. "Thank you." He nodded and left. My heart was pounding, which is ridiculous.

That night I wrote it in the note. There are thirty-one things on it now. On bad days I scroll through it. It doesn't make me arrogant. It makes me steadier.

qa.q: How many things are on Vinita's note now?
qa.a: There are thirty-one things on it now.

qa.q: Why was Vinita's heart pounding when she simply said "thank you"?
qa.a: Accepting praise without deflecting felt risky and unfamiliar, as if she were claiming too much. Breaking a long habit, even a small one, felt big.

qa.q: What does Vinita's approach show about letting good things count?
qa.a: Saying thank you and recording facts helped her confidence rest on evidence rather than doubt. She says it makes her steadier, not arrogant.

qa.q: How might Tejas have experienced Vinita's simple "thank you"?
qa.a: Tejas probably felt his compliment was received, which is pleasant for the person giving it. If she'd argued, he might have felt awkward for praising her.

grounding: A young woman practises simply thanking people for compliments and keeps a private list of achievements, which steadies her confidence.

School counsellor's note, Class 9, Thursday

Ayesha, 14, was sent to me after her maths teacher found her copying from Keerthana's paper during the unit test. It was two answers, both word for word.

Ayesha spoke quickly and firmly. "Mrs Raman is the strictest teacher in the school. Half the questions weren't even from the chapter. Everyone copies in her tests, I just got caught." She added, twice, "I'm not a cheater. I'm a good student. Ask anyone."

When I asked what she had done in the test, she looked at the window for a long time.

I think she is holding on to the story that she's a good person who was treated unfairly, because the alternative feels unbearable right now. That picture of herself matters to her, which is actually a good starting point.

Next step: I'll meet her again tomorrow, and help her think about how a good student might put right a mistake, including speaking to Mrs Raman herself.

I'm Jahnavi. In my first job at a travel company, my manager, Rafiq, called me on a Tuesday and said, "Change the brochure. Put the hill stations first, beaches after." I did it that afternoon.

On Friday, in the team meeting, he held up the printed brochure. "Why are the beaches second? I clearly said beaches first. Jahnavi, young lady, you must have misunderstood."

My face burned. I knew what he'd said. I also knew I had no proof. The call was just a call.

I didn't argue in the meeting. But that evening I started a habit I still keep. After every instruction by phone or in person, I send a short, polite email: "Just confirming: hill stations first, beaches second. Will proceed on this basis."

Two months later it happened again, with a price list. This time I calmly forwarded my email. He read it, cleared his throat and said, "Ah. Let's go with what we agreed."

He never apologised. But he stopped saying I'd misunderstood.

qa.a: "Change the brochure. Put the hill stations first, beaches after."

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when her face burned in the Friday meeting?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and wronged, knowing she had followed his instructions but being made to look careless in front of the team. Having no proof made it worse.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi's confirmation emails work so well?
qa.a: They gave a calm, written record of what was agreed, so when Rafiq changed his story she could show the facts without accusing him. It protected her without a fight.

qa.q: Why might Rafiq have said Jahnavi misunderstood, rather than admitting he changed his mind?
qa.a: Admitting the change might make him feel like a poor manager in front of the team. Blaming Jahnavi let him keep his image, even though it was unfair to her.

grounding: A young employee is told she misunderstood after her manager changed his instructions, and learns to protect herself by calmly keeping written records.

The youth club in Kumarakom met on the temple verandah after the evening lamp. Joseph, the club secretary, had the attendance register open on his knees.

For three years he had insisted that the village football tournament be held in May, "the way our fathers did it." Every year Reena, the treasurer, had suggested moving it to December. Every year he'd said no.

Tonight he read out the numbers. Teams: eleven, then eight, then five. Spectators: fewer each year. Two players had fainted in the heat last May.

He closed the register. "I was wrong," he said. "Reena was right. I kept May because I didn't want to change what I'd defended. That was pride."

A few people shifted. Somebody coughed.

"So here's what changes," Joseph said. "This year, the tournament is in December. Reena, can you and I visit the other villages together next week and invite their teams back?"

Reena smiled. "Next Sunday."

qa.a: By saying clearly he was wrong and naming the change, Joseph gave credit to Reena and a fresh start to the club. A little pride lost now can save the tournament.

I'm Bhavna. When I was nine, Kunal in my class had scented erasers shaped like fruits. The strawberry one smelled like real strawberries.

One day at break I took it and put it in my pencil box. When he looked for it, I said, "Oh, I'm just borrowing it."

I didn't give it back that day, or the next. Every time I said "borrowing" in my head, it felt okay, like a normal thing friends do.

Then Kunal started calling me "Strawberry Thief". I told Miss it was mean. Miss asked me, "Bhavna, when did you plan to give it back?"

I didn't have an answer. I'd never planned to.

I gave it back the next morning and said sorry. Kunal said sorry for the name too.

Now I notice when I say "just". Just borrowing. Just joking. It's usually covering something.

qa.a: When Miss asked when Bhavna planned to give it back, and Bhavna realised there had never been a plan. The question showed what the word "borrowing" had been covering.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt while the eraser was missing?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt annoyed and upset that his favourite eraser was gone, which may be why he started the mean nickname. Hearing "just borrowing" wouldn't have made losing it feel any better.

grounding: A child takes a classmate's eraser and calls it just borrowing, a softer word that makes the act feel harmless until a teacher's question shows it.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, Monday

For two weeks Varun has been calling Nitin "Idli-face" because Nitin brings idlis most days. Others have joined in. Today Nitin didn't open his tiffin at all.

When I spoke to Varun, he laughed. "It's just a joke, Miss. Nitin laughs too."

"Did Nitin laugh today?"

He thought. "...No."

"It's just a joke," he said again, more quietly. The word seems to make it feel like something that just happens, not something he chose.

I asked him to look across at Nitin, sitting alone with his closed tiffin. Varun watched for a while and stopped smiling.

Next step: I'll talk with both boys together tomorrow, call Nitin's mother today, and hold a class talk this week about when a joke stops being one.

qa.q: What did Nitin do with his tiffin today?
qa.a: Nitin didn't open his tiffin at all.

qa.q: Why does Varun keep repeating "It's just a joke"?
qa.a: Varun seems uncomfortable once Nitin's silence is pointed out, and repeating "just a joke" helps him feel the teasing was harmless and not really his choice.

qa.q: What turning point did the teacher create, and what should happen next?
qa.a: Asking Varun to look at Nitin sitting alone with his closed tiffin, which made him stop smiling. Next, talking with both boys and Nitin's mother the same day helps make sure it stops.

qa.q: What is lunchtime like for Nitin now?
qa.a: Nitin seems to feel ashamed of his own food, sitting alone without opening his tiffin. The nickname has turned lunch into something to dread.

grounding: A teacher notes a boy who calls cruel teasing just a joke, a softer word that makes it feel harmless and less of his own choice.

passage:
At the government school in Barmer, the boys waited for the bus under the only tree in the yard. Every afternoon for three weeks, Vikas and his friends had the same routine for Deepak, whose father sold vegetables from a cart. "Oi, sabziwala! Any tomatoes today?" "Deepak smells of onions!"

Deepak always stood a little apart, looking at the road.

Today the Hindi teacher, waiting for her own bus, heard it. "Vikas. Enough."

"Ma'am, it's just banter," Vikas said, grinning. "Everyone jokes like that here. Deepak doesn't mind. Right, Deepak?"

Deepak didn't answer. He was gripping his bag strap so tightly his knuckles were pale.

"Everyone jokes," Vikas repeated, a little less sure. "It's normal."

The bus came. Deepak got on first and went to the very back, alone, and looked out of the window the whole way.

Vikas sat with his friends and laughed at something else. He didn't look back.

qa.q: What did Deepak's father sell?
qa.a: Vegetables from a cart.

qa.q: Why does calling it "banter" make it easier for Vikas to carry on?
qa.a: The word makes the comments sound normal and harmless, so he doesn't have to think of them as hurting someone. It hides how Deepak feels behind the idea that everyone jokes.

qa.q: What could the Hindi teacher do next so this doesn't continue?
qa.a: She could speak to Vikas and his friends separately, ask them to notice how Deepak reacts, and let Deepak's class teacher and parents know. Checking on Deepak privately matters too.

qa.q: What is the bus ride home like for Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak seems hurt and alone, sitting at the very back and staring out of the window. The pale knuckles and silence show he minds a great deal, whatever Vikas claims.

grounding: A teenage boy calls weeks of nasty comments about a classmate's family banter and says everyone jokes like that, hiding how the target feels.

passage:
In the class group chat at their school in Oslo, Oskar posted another one: a video of himself doing an exaggerated version of Sofia's accent, rolling every r. "Sofia explaining photosynthesis lol" Six people reacted with laughing faces.

It was the fourth this month. Sofia had moved from Chile a year ago.

The next morning, his friend Lars said quietly, "Maybe stop with the Sofia videos?"

"Come on, it's banter," Oskar said. "We all do it. She makes fun of my handwriting."

"Once. Months ago."

"Everyone jokes like that. If she didn't like it, she'd say so."

Across the corridor, Sofia was at her locker. She'd left the group chat the night before, though nobody had noticed. When the teacher called on her in biology, she said, "I don't know," although her notebook had the answer written out.

Oskar didn't see any of that. To him it was still just banter.

qa.q: How many people reacted with laughing faces?
qa.a: Six people.

qa.q: Why does Oskar say "If she didn't like it, she'd say so"?
qa.a: Oskar feels defensive, so assuming Sofia would speak up lets him believe the videos are harmless fun and avoid noticing how she actually feels.

qa.q: What could Oskar do if he listened to Lars?
qa.a: Stop posting the videos, delete the old ones, and apologise to Sofia directly. Paying attention to her quiet reactions would show him it isn't banter to her.

qa.q: What does Sofia's "I don't know" in biology suggest about her experience?
qa.a: It suggests Sofia now avoids speaking in class so her accent won't be mocked, even when she knows the answer. The videos have made her quieter and more alone.

grounding: A teenage boy calls repeated mocking videos of a classmate's accent banter and says everyone jokes like that, while the target quietly withdraws.
